transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. How can I help you today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. I'm here because I spend so much time trying to fix how I look before I go out that I end up missing things with my family and at work. It's gotten to the point where it's really affecting my life, and I'm honestly pretty embarrassed to even admit it.
Can you describe what specific concerns you have about your appearance, and what kinds of things you do to fix or check them?

I'm constantly convinced that my nose is crooked, my skin is saggy and blotchy, and my jaw is drooping. Because of this, I'll spend over an hour staring in the mirror, changing shirts, zooming in on photos, and constantly asking my daughter or coworkers if I look weird. I get so worked up trying to fix everything under different lighting that I end up running terribly late or just canceling entirely.
Do you think these appearance issues might be exaggerated or not completely accurate, even though they feel very real when you're focused on them?

People always tell me I look fine for my age, but it feels completely real to me. When I look in the mirror, all I can see is this lopsided, older face with saggy skin and a crooked nose. It's really hard for me to believe that these concerns are exaggerated when they look so obvious to me.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["F45.2", "F63.3"], but based on this conversation, F63.3 (excoriation disorder) seems unlikely because the patient is not reporting any skin-picking behavior or similar repetitive self-grooming actions that result in tissue damage. Instead, the patient describes excessive preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance (e.g., crooked nose, saggy skin), repetitive checking and reassurance-seeking behaviors, significant distress, functional impairment, and poor insight—believing the flaws are real despite others' reassurance. These features are characteristic of body dysmorphic disorder, which corresponds to F45.2. No other ICD-10 codes are currently supported by the clinical picture.

inference_history.note: Previously the candidates were ["F45.2", "F63.3", "F42"], but based on this conversation, F42 (obsessive-compulsive disorder) is less likely because the patient's repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, seeking reassurance, adjusting appearance) are driven by a preoccupation with perceived physical flaws rather than intrusive thoughts or compulsions unrelated to body image. The focus on specific appearance concerns (nose, skin, jaw) and time-consuming rituals to fix them aligns more strongly with a body image disorder. F45.2 (hypochondriacal disorder) remains relevant due to the persistent preoccupation with physical appearance, though it typically refers to health concerns rather than appearance per se. F63.3 (dysmorphophobia) is highly consistent with the clinical picture of excessive concern over imagined or minor defects in appearance, leading to significant functional impairment. Thus, F42 is dropped and the current candidates are F45.2 and F63.3.
